Mr. Speaker, we will have a further opportunity of discussing this particular clause in committee. Once more, allow me to say that I disassociate myself entirely from the remarks made by the hon. member (Mr. Pardee) that we should lay aside all of those things whmh had their influence when the War-time Elections Act and the Military Voters' Act were passed. In considering the future of Canada may I be permitted to say that in my judgment we should he mote particular in handing out the franchise than we have ever been in the past? May I say that in my .udgment one of the great weaknesses in our Franchise Acts in this country is that we have opened the door too wide. We have cared nothing whether a man understood a word of the English language or not, or whether he understood anything of British principles or of our constitution. So long as he was twenty-one years of age he was allowed to vote and so enjoyed as free an exercise of the franchise as a man who thoroughly understood the principles of Government under which we live.
'In my judgment that is wrong and I think it has been a weakness in our legislation in this country. If those people come to Canada from other countries they do so because they believe the conditions here are better than the conditions in the country of their birth. That being the case I say that they should in some way show that they possess some knowledge of our country and of our principles of government before they are put on an equal footing with people who were born and raised in Canada and upon whom in a time of crisis the responsibility of "carrying on" devolves. I say, Sir, with respect to any person or to any class of people in Canada who during the last four or five years proved by their attitude that they were not prepared to assume all the responsibilities of citizenship, that I am not ready for one, simply because the war is over, to tell them that they can come in and have as much voice in the administration of the affairs of this country for the next five or ten



years as those persons who assumed and worthily bore their full share of responsibility. That is my attitude and I believe it will appeal with greater force to the people of Canada than the attitude which has been stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) and so vigorously endorsed by those who sit around him.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
I will not attempt, Mr. Speaker, to answer bitter words with bitter words. The occasion which calls us together this evening is of far too great importance for us to take up the country's time in bandying doubtful compliments across the floor of the Chamber. I rise for the purpose of supporting the spirit of the remarks offered by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) and I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to the manner in which other countries that have suffered just as much as we have-aye, and far more-in the conflict which has closed are treating this subject of after the war reconstruction. This Bill is a part of after the war reconstruction, for what we are discussing tonight is the charter under which Canadian society shall operate in the future.
Let us turn for a moment to Italy. I suppose there are few nations in the world that have suffered as Italy has suffered under the awful tyranny imposed upon her for generations by Austria. During the war Italy suffered frightfully; her northern provinces, some of the fairest she possesses, were overwhelmed by Austrian and German troops. A poor country with a tremendous debt before the war, her debt is now of crushing magnitude. Life will be harder and more bitter on account of the war for the population of Italy for years to come. But what is Italy doing to-day, Mr. Speaker? Italy in her poverty is taking tens of thousands of starving Austrian children and entertaining them in her own homes. That is the spirit in which the uoild can be reconstructed for a better future; but the spirit shown by some hon. rcembtrs is just the opposite.
What is Great Britain doing? I would suppose all will admit that the part played in the war by Great Britain, by those little islands in the North sea, has been just as fine as the part played by Canada. I would imagine that all hon. members will agree with me when I state that the losses of young British manhood have been as heavy, aye, heavier than our own. Why, Scotland, the place from which my forbears came, has lost such a proportion of

her young manhood as would make the angels weep. What is Great Britain doing? To-day perhaps the one solvent country in Europe, through the Economic Council of the Allies at Paris she is proposing to make advances to Germany in order to allow that country to get on its feet.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: That is not votes.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
No, but that is the
spirit which should animate us to-day. Now, in that spirit I shall ask all hon. members to approach this matter-not animated by hate, for, as the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) said the other day, we cannot build up a new world on hate; we must build it up on love. Is it a strange doctrine to say that one must love his enemies? It is a doctrine that has been preached for two hundred years-:

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
Oh, oh. Two
thousand years.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
We may well laugh,
because although it has been preached for two thousand years it has never been followed in international politics. The great fundamental reason for the Gethsemane through which humanity has passed during the last five years was that those principles were not adopted. And I ask this House and this country to approach this subject in the proper spirit-and we all know what that proper spirit is.
Let me ask this question also. Did those in our community from whom the right to vote is taken by this Bill-our people of Austrian origin-behave themselves badly during that period? I cannot speak from personal experience. I know there are very few German or Austrian people in Montreal, and there are none in my constituency; but as far as I know they gave no succour to the enemy, but behaved themselves in seemly and proper fashion; and from the information I have received I understand that in other parts of the country those belonging especially to the Austrian nation, Hungarians and Bohemians, were not only not anti-British or anti-Ally, they were pro-Ally, and volunteered in large numbers to fight for the Allies. Have there been plots in Canada by our German population? I do not think so. I believe I should have heard of them had there been any.
But, after all, I ask: How are we going to build up a Canadian people? It seems to me that there are only two courses to pursue:	If a man is not a desirable citi-

zen, he should be asked on fair terms to leave the country; and if he is a desirable citizen, then he should be given all the privileges and responsibilities of citizenship. I know no other way by which you can build up a great nation.
Before I sit down I wish to deal further with the principle of the Bill. By section 30, subsection one (g) it is provided that:
Persons who, by the laws of any province in Canada, are disqualified from voting for a member of the Legislative Assembly of such province in respect of race, shall not be qualified to vote in such province under the provisions of this Act.
To this provision I take strong exception. I do not think it is wise, nor do I think it is honourable. This is our Act-the Act of the Dominion of Canada. Naturalization papers are given by this Government-the federal Government. Once we give naturalization to people, no matter whence they come, they must be given full rights, and those rights include the right inherent in Canadian citizenship-the right to vote. We cannot have different grades of citizenship. What is this provision aimed at? It is because certain provinces, for reason which perhaps appears just to themselves, have withheld the provincial franchise from men and women of Oriental origin. Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to discuss the wisdom or unwisdom of having orientals settle in this country, for it is not a question on which I would feel qualified to speak without giving it profound study. But that is not the question affected by the Bill. What the Bill affects is Canadian citizens, and the proposal is to take from Canadian naturalized citizens the right to vote,-the most precious right of citizenship. And when you consider, Sir, who are being disfranchised under this clause, its ignobleness, if I may use the expression, is startling. Who protected our Pacific. coast when the war was on? The cruisers of Great Britain's ally, Japan. Who are being disfranchised by this Bill? The former subjects of the Mikado. Is that gratitude? A certain political and moral philosopher has said: What is not good morals cannot be good politics. This is not good morals for it is base ingratitude; and it cannot be regarded as good politics.
I am no Imperialist, Mr. Speaker, but I have a very warm regard for the Mother Country, and a strong desire to help her in every way I can, and I say that an Act such as this passed by the Parliament of the second, if not the first, of the members of the Britannic Commonwealth, the Dominion of Canada, cannot but tend to hurt the 47i
relationship which should exist between Great Britain and her great Eastern ally, Japan.
And who also is attacked by this Bill? Our fellow-British subjects from India. What did they do in the war? They, of another race, of another colour, sent-from a population of teeming millions, it is true-into what was essentially a white man's war,
1,500,000	men. They fought on the Western front; they fought in Egypt; they fought in Mesopotamia,-but they are not to vote in British Columbia. Is that right? Oh, you may say, you must not offend the feelings of British Columbia. I do not want to offend the feelings of British Columbia.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: You are doing it.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
The member for West Toronto says that I am doing it. When the war broke out a Home Rule Bill had been passed in the Imperial Parliament, but in order not to offend Ulster that Home Rule Bill was postponed; it was put into the cupboard and allowed to get stale. What was the result of that desire not to offend Ulster? It was the rebellion of Easter, 1916, and it is the existence of the Irish question, fhe greatest and the most serious question that faces the British Empire today. You have to offend sometimes in order to do what is right. Surely the member for West Toronto has never hesitated to offend when he thought that to do so was necessary to the accomplishing of something that he thought good.
But, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to conclude my remarks in a tone of bitterness or on the plane of conflict. I ask that the members of this House consider this Bill seriously, carefully and well, remembering that when you have your enemy in the dust, to rub his face in the dirt, or, as this Bill proposes, to rub his thirty-second cousin's face in the dirt, is poor business, poor politics, poor statesmanship.
Mr. WILLIAM D. EULER (Waterloo North): Mr. Speaker it had been my intention to discuss certain phases of this Bill in Committee of the Whole, but the debate has taken a certain turn which impels to discuss the matter just a little more broadly than I could discuss it within the rules under any clause in committee and it is for that reason that I am going to make my observations now.
It is not my intention, although the provocation is great, to answer insult with insult. It is my intention to debate a certain principle, or the violation of a certain

principle, in this Bill from the point of view entirely of logic and justice and fair play. If I cannot convince the Government and members on the other side of the justice of my argument in a reasonable and logical way, I am assuredly not going to make an appeal to sentiment, because I think the time for that has pretty well passed.
Before I proceed further, may I say that I hope the Government will use the machinery which it is about to provide, and in connection with which certain amendments will, I trust, be made, to give the people of this country an opportunity of using it in the election of a Parliament that properly represents them.
I shall confine myself entirely to those clauses of the Bill which most closely touch the people in the riding which I have the honour to represent. I may say frankly that I am going to discuss to-night the attempt to disfranchise British subjects of late enemy origin,-or, if you like, of British subjects in Canada who are of German or Austrian birth. And I want to say that I am not on my feet to make a plea for the alien. I am not going to make a plea for any one; I am merely going to demand a square deal for men who are British subjects and good citizens of Canada.
I think, Sir, it is also in order for me to point out that in its application, the word " alien " has been abused in this House ever since I entered it. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House-perhaps hon. gentlemen on this side have occasionally done so-have frequently spoken in debate of " aliens," when they meant men of alien origin. I contend that when a man has become a naturalized British subject he is no longer an alien; he is in very truth a British subject, and entitled to the privileges of a British subject.
I realize, Sir, that in discussing these particular clauses in the Bill I am in a somewhat peculiar position. I appreciate that perhaps I am the only member of this House whose ancestors sprang from the race with which we have been at war. As is probably well known

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: The member for Edmonton.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of any other member of the House who is' of the same descent as I am. But whether there is another or not, I want to say that on that score I have no apology whatever to make, because before I am through I think I shall be able to show that, after all, 
I am in very good company. I should like to say also that I was born in this country, ' and that I am a Canadian. I would like hon. members as they listen to me to-night to remember, if possible, for the purposes of this debate that I am a Canadian as they are, and to give me credit, as I give credit to them, for a desire to serve my country, Canada. If they are able to do that I shall appreciate it.
Sir, I had hoped that the Franchise Bill when it was introduced into this House would be free from the objectionable clauses which obtained in the War-time Elections Act. It is not my purpose to indulge in any lengthy recriminations with regard to that Act. It has been described as a blot on the statute book of Canada. For my part I should be glad to see it relegated to the limbo of forgotten things, together with other scraps of paper, and other broken agreements. But I did hope after the minister spoke the other day that the Bill would be almost entirely free from the disfranchising clauses of the War-time Elections Act.
I know that the impression prevails throughout the country, fostered by the press, and justifiably so, I believe from the information that we had, that the Franchise Bill, which is now before the House, is a very fair measure, and that perhaps very little fault can be found with it. But a careful study of the Bill, together with a study of some of the provisions of the Naturalization Act passed last year, discloses the fact that this Bill will disfranchise many more British subjects than were disfranchised under the War-time Elections Act. Indeed, I think it is almost true to say that while the War-time Elections Act disfranchised its thousands, this Act as it stands will disfranchise its tens of thousands.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: Under what provision of this Act does my hon. friend justify the statement he has just made?

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
I am coming to that, and if I am wrong I shall be very glad to be corrected, and my remarks will come to a conclusion very quickly. I am going on with this more particularly now because the charges made by my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) were much the same as I am about to make, though perhaps my remarks may be made from another viewpoint. No exception was taken to the statements of the hon. member for West Lambton. In fact, hon. gentlemen opposite seemed to believe that what

he charged was the intent and meaning of the Act.
To make my point clear I want to state certain definite facts. The first is expressed in the Naturalization Act of 1919, section 11:
The wife of a British subject shall be deemed to be a British subject.
That is all that is necessary for me to quote for the purpose of my argument. Secondly, the children of a naturalized alien, being minors, both male and female, become naturalized quite legally with the naturalization of the father. The result therefore is that the naturalization of a father of alien origin naturalizes his wife and his children of both sexes. I think that is the case. At least, that was the law up until the Act of 1914, and even since that Act was passed the children are still naturalized under the law, provided they are mentioned in the naturalization certificate. That I understand is the purport of the law.
The next fact I would mention is this: The Bill gives the franchise to women; that is well known. Secondly-and this is one of the most important facts of all-before these wives and children of naturalized aliens can be permitted to vote, although they are in very truth British subjects- and I want to emphasize that-the Bill before the House states very definitely that they must obtain personal naturalization. I will read the section for the purposes of record. Subsection2 of section 29 says:
For the purposes of this Act, the allegiance or nationality of a person, as it was at the birth of such person shall be deemed incapable of being changed, or of having been changed, merely by reason or in consequence of marriage or change of allegiance or naturalization of any other person,-
Such other person being the father, I presume.
-or otherwise than by personal naturalization of such first mentioned person.
I think that makes it perfectly clear that all these British subjects, being the wives or grown-up children of duly naturalized men of alien origin, cannot vote under this Bill unless they become personally naturalized through the Secretary of State. Finally, and this is just as important as what I have already mentioned, the Naturalization Act of 1919 provides (Part II, section 8, subsection 4, (b):
No certificate of naturalization shall, before the expiration of a period of ten years after the termination of the present war, be granted in Canada, to any subject of a country which at the time of the passing of this Act was at war with His Majesty.
Then follow certain exceptions. Thus the joint effect of these clauses is to disfranchise thousands of women and men of German or Austrian birth. Now if there is any escape from what I have said, it must be through an interpretation of this clause. The clause is not absolutely clear to me, but it is certainly capable of being interpreted in the way I have indicated. If I have interpreted it incorrectly I should be very glad if the Solicitor General would set me right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: The last part of my hon. friend's interpretation I think is absolutely correct. The Naturalization Act of 1919 provides that no subject of any enemy state shall be permitted to be naturalized in this country for a period of ten years after the close of the war. That would include Austrians, Germans, Bulgars, and Turks. They will not under the present Bill be entitled to vote, nor will they under the Naturalization Act be entitled to become British subjects for a period of ten years from the end of the war. That is correct.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: I think the minister has missed my point. The point I am trying to make is this: British subjects, naturalized in Canada by virtue of the naturalization of some one else, either husband or father, must under the Bill before the House obtain personal naturalization in order to vote, and my interpretation is that they cannot obtain naturalization because of the clause I have just read. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: They cannot if they are Austrians, Germans, Bulgars or Turks. That is absolutely correct.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: Exactly. I am referring to naturalized British subjects of Austrian or German birth who have become naturalized by virtue of their fathers' .or husbands' naturalization. I am correct then in stating that people originally of these races, though now British subjects-and I want again to emphasize that point-cannot obtain personal naturalization under the Act of 1919.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: No, they cannot for ten years.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
I am quite sure they cannot, because I took occasion to investigate and made inquiry of the Under-Secretary of State. I put this question to him: "What would you do if a British subject, of German or Austrian birth, who had become naturalized by reason of the naturalization of father

or husband, applied for personal naturalization?" He replied "Naturalization would be refused." So that point seems perfectly clear.
Let me review these points. We have, I think, in the Dominion of Canada, about
115,000	of male naturalized citizens of former enemy alien origin. My figures may not be exactly correct, but they are nearly so. These people are British subjects, although of German or Austrian birth. Secondly, this Bill says they cannot vote unless they become personally naturalized. Thirdly, the Naturalization Act forbids such naturalization. Therefore it is a fact that if the Bill passes as drafted, probably something like 100,000 British subjects in Canada will be deprived of the right to vote at the next election, and perhaps for a period of ten years altogether.
' When the Naturalization Act was piloted through the House last session by the Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Guthrie), it will be recalled that I objected very strongly to the ten-year clause, and made the argument then that credit should be given at least to those people who had already lived in Canada for ten, fifteen, thirty, forty or even fifty years. I was unable to carry my point, although as a matter of fact the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) said he was in sympathy with the stand I had taken in view of the fact that both he and the President of the Privy Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell), had so expressed themselves at the Peace conference in Paris. However, for various reasons, the suggestion was not adopted and I was unsuccessful in securing the result I desired. At that time it did seem to me that the reasons given for failure to adopt my suggestion were trivial and insufficient; and if I were of a suspicious nature, which I am not, I would be apt to surmise that the action of the Government last session in placing that ten-year clause in the Naturalization Act was committed with a pre-vision of what was to follow in the Franchise Bill which we have now before us. I do not say that I believe this to have been the case, but 1 say that if I were suspicious I would be apt to think that it was then the intention to disfranchise these people.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend must remember the discussion of last year, and he no doubt knows that the Bill which this House passed then is the accepted model in all British colonies, being the Act in force in the Motherland, and applies to

British citizenship, not only in Canada but through the British Empire. The ten-year clause in the Imperial Act, which we followed.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
In reply to that statement of the hon. gentleman, let me say that the Prime Minister on the floor of the House, after I had drawn his attention to his own speech at the Peace conference, which he admitted embodied his sentiments in this regard, said:
I assure my hon. friend that I will make representations to the British Government with respect to the matter with a view to having such modifications made in the Imperial Act as will permit of reasonable modifications In our own.
I communicated with the Prime Minister, not long ago, inquiring of him whether he had done as he had promised, and he replied that he was taking the matter up with the Solicitor General. I am informed, however, that nothing whatever has been done in that direction, and I am forced to the conclusion that there never was any intention that anything should be done.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if it were worth while, we might compare the present Franchise Bill with the War-time Elections Act. In the War-time Elections Act there was not the degree of disfranchising that will-occur under this Act, by which every woman of German or Austrian birth will be deprived of a vote in the coming elections. And if I may be allowed a personal remark, I may say that this Act, if it passes, will disfranchise my mother, although she has lived in Canada as a good Canadian citizen, having reared good Canadians, for sixty years. It will deprive of the franchise all women who have lived in this country for many years, but who were born in Germany and were naturalized as a result of the naturalization of their fathers. But observe the injustice of this, Mr. Speaker. Many of those whom this Act will disfranchise have actually voted in past years, having been duly naturalized British subjects. Under this Act, if it is read with the Naturalization Act, they are deprived of the right to vote by reason of the ten-year clause. I know that there are in the riding I represent men who have lived in that locality during the past few years perfectly secuie and serene in the belief that their franchise would not be imperilled, because they had complied with the requirements of the law in that they had become naturalized with the naturalization of their fathers. They have no remedy now. There can be no doubt in the mind

of any hon. gentleman that if these men had for one moment suspected that a law would be passed depriving them of the franchise, unless they obtained personal naturalization, they would long ago have taken steps to obtain such naturalization. Now, under the law, it is utterly impossible for them to do so. The Acting Solicitor General this afternoon spoke of anomalies which might arise if certain suggestions were adopted. I think one of them was that if the women of Quebec had not been given the franchise we should have the peculiar position of a woman of the province of Quebec being able to stand as a candidate for Parliament and yet not have the vote. I wonder if we aTe not in exactly that position to-day. These women and men who are disfranchised are still British subjects although they have not got the vote. Now Sir, the requirement of a candidate for the Canadian House of Commons is that he or she shall be a British subject of the age of twenty-one years. It may be that my constituency in its wisdom will select some good honest Canadian woman of German birth, a British subject, and will send that woman to the Canadian Parliament although she herself will have no vote. There are other anomalies in the Act as it stands, and as I believe that the minister was sincere this afternoon when he said that if necessary corrections were pointed out to him he would adopt them, I think after I have indicated some of these anomalies he will feel inclined to effect some changes.
This clause will enfranchise men who could not vote in the war-time election; it will enfranchise those men who were disfranchised in the last election if they had been naturalized within the last fifteen years and were of enemy origin. It will disfranchise men who had votes in the wartime elections. Now, you have this peculiar situation:	Men of alien origin who could
not vote under war conditions will be allowed to vote now that we have peace, and men who were allowed to vote in war time will not he permitted this privilege in the future. That, surely, is an anomaly of the first order. I desire to refer to another important point. I have not read the Act as closely as I should like to have done, but so far as I can see there is absolutely no provision giving the franchise to women of German or Austrian birth, British subjects, who gave their sons to the war, even if those sons were killed. I find no provision enabling such women to vote; and in reply to some statements made by
another hon. member, I beg to give to the House just a little bit of proof that the German Canadians, British subjects in Canada, were not quite so remiss in their duty in this war as some people would have us suppose.
I have in my hand a list of men who were killed in the war, all of whom came from the city of Kitchener, or the town of Waterloo, and possibly a few from other parts of the riding. I shall not read all the names hut I am going to read some of them, and I think that when you hear me pronounce them you will have no doubt whatever as to their racial origin. The first is Lieutenant Harry Snyder, a young man whom I had the honour to instruct when I was a public school teacher in the schools of what was then Berlin, now the city of Kitchener. That young man enlisted, entered the air force, was some time later reported as missing and has never been heard of since. I spoke to a brother of his last Sunday just before leaving for Ottawa. I mentioned the Franchise Act and this disfranchising provision. He said to me: "It will disfranchise my mother who gave her son." That is one case. Then there are Private Zapfe, and Private Schreiter, Private J. Gehl, Private Knechtel, Private G. Stuffer, who is a descendant of the Mennonites of whom we have heard so much; Private A. . Sehierholtz, Private George Strub, Private J. Gerbig, Private Y. Hummel, Private J. Diefen-becker, Private H. Rosenberger, Private H. Treusch, Private S. Uffelman, Private Herman Gross, Private Clayton Fenner, Private Steckenraider, and Lieutenant W. Bauer. These men gave up their lives fighting in the armies of Canada. I do not know to what extent that clause will affect their mothers. I do know it will affect the mothers in some cases at least and I believe it will affect the sisters of some of these men. I referred a moment ago to the fact that some twenty years ago I had the privilege of teaching in the public schools in the city of Kitchener. Besides teaching the ordinary subjects of the public' school course, I did what I could to inculcate in those boys and girls a measure of patriotism and of faith in British institutions. I taught those boys and girls that British law and institutions stood for justice and fair play. I believed then what I taught. After the record of the last four or five years and sometimes as I have listened to speeches and statements made in this House, that faith of mine has occasionally wavered and as a result of certain incidents has continued to do so. If

that clause is retained in the Bill, certainly my confidence in the justice of the British people in this House will not be strengthened.
The boys and girls Of the city of Kitchener-and I speak particularly of that city because I live there and because there is in that city a large admixture of people oi German origin,-are still being taught to be good citizens. They are told that Canada is a progressive country. They are told that the women of Canada have been given the franchise. I have no doubt that those boys and girls come from homes in whieh there are fathers and mothers who, perhaps, forty, fifty or sixty years ago, were born in Germany or Austria. : They will tell the mothers that they also have received the franchise. When election day comes the mother will have to learn that under this law she has no vote. The father goes to vote because he is enfranchised again; he has his personal naturalization papers. I can fancy that the girls and boys will urge the mother also to go and vote because, I believe, our public schools are teaching the children that one of the greatest privileges and duties they may have is the right to exercise the franchise. The mother must say to them that she cannot vote. The inevitable question comes: "Why not"? The answer is that because thirty, forty or fifty years ago she was born in Germany or Austria. " But," says the boy, "father was born in Germany and he can vote; why not mother"? Do you think that any reply the father or mother can make will satisfy the sense of justice of those Canadian boys and girls? What will be the effect upon those boys? Will they despise the mother who is insulted, or will they look with contempt upon the law and the Government which did the wrong?
Let me take another concrete case. A father and a mother came from Germany, for example, thirty years ago, both of them being, we will say, thirty years of age. They brought with them a boy of five and a girl of three. In four or five years the father obtains. Canadian naturalization in the regular way. In the course of two or three years another boy and another daughter are born to this couple. We have now the passing of this Act with an election following. The young people who were born in Canada are British subjects; the older ones are also British subjects. The younger ones do not require to be naturalized personally because they were horn on Canadian soil. They have now reached voting age. The older son has been voting for twelve or four-

teen years. An election comes on and under this Act you have this condition; that the father, the younger son and the younger daughter go to the polls and vote while the mother and the older son, who in the past has been voting, and the older sister, are compelled to remain at home. In addition to that, it is not at all a far-fetched Suggestion that the younger son, whose mother, older sister and older brother are disfranchised, may have fought in the war as a volunteer recruit in the Canadian army.
I think it would be impossible to conceive of anything more illogical, more unfair, and, if I may use a word that is unparliamentary-that is more tricky or more calculated to destroy faith in the national decency and honour than this proposal. The Wartime Elections Act was bad. But in the War-time Elections Act of 1917 the entry was made by the front door and the right of British subjects was taken away openly. By the Bill we have now before us, entrance is made by the back door of the Naturalization Act with the apparent idea that the plunder may be abstracted before those who are robbed know what has happened to them.
Mr. Speaker, there must be reasons for this legislation and I can conceive of only three, one of which perhaps I must already discard. The first one is that possibly the Government did not quite appreciate what the joint effect of these two clauses would be. I can hardly believe that to be the case because apparently the effect is quite intentional, being so admitted by the Acting Solicitor General. The second possible reason is that the Government felt that these people should be disfranchised in the interests of Canada itself. And the third reason that occurs to me is that these people are disfranchised in order to gain a political advantage.
Now let us examine the second. What can be said or has been said, to show that the granting of the franchise to these British subjects could prejudice the interests of Canada? The war is over, and I do not think it is the intention of the Canadian Government to prepare for another war with Germany or Austria or any other country; at all events I devoutly hope not. I do not see, under those conditions, how the vote of these women, cast in a Canadian election for members of the House of Commons, could possibly be injurious to Canada.
Let us examine the conduct of the people who are affected by this law. The question has been asked by hon, gentlemen on this

side, how have these people 'behaved? I can speak only for those ol North Waterloo, and while I am very well awaTe that a great many comments have been made about that blessed portion of this Dominion, a great deal of what has been said has not been true. If I might again be permitted a personal remark I would say that in the first year of the war I happened to have the honour of being mayor of the city of Kitchener. That city was one of the very first to organize -a branch of the Canadian Patriotic Fund, and its people, who are largely of German origin, voluntarily contributed individually and through the municipality, at that time a larger sum per capita than did any other centre in Canada. They gave liberally also to the Red Cross, the British Red Cross Society, and they subscribed most generously to the Victory Loan, as the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) will know. Again, in 1918 I think, the riding of North Waterloo subscribed a larger per capita percentage of the loan than did any other riding in the province of Ontario with the exception of those situated in the larger centres of population. Further, the number of voluntary enlistments compares favourably with those of many other parts of Canada.
If these people were disloyal, if they were acting as traitors-as one hon. gentleman opposite suggested-how is it that we have had no prosecutions? I may be wrong but I am pretty well acquainted with the facts in the county of Waterloo, and especially in the riding of North Waterloo, and I cannot recall that there was even one successful prosecution of a British subject of the kind I am discussing for treasonable utterances or anything that could be construed as disloyal. I want to say also that there are a great many people in that county who, if anything of the kind had been practised, would very soon have taken action, and punishment would have followed. Speaking of internments, British subjects, of course, could not be interned without a trial. There were about eight thousand internments in the whole Dominion, but with the exception of one, so far as I know, the persons interned were all alien enemies who are not the subject of this debate at all. In this connection I want it to be clearly understood that the people of whom I am speaking to-night are not alien enemies; they are people of alien birth but they are British subjects. Of these there was not one convicted, not one man was interned. I should perhaps make an exception. There were ^even
internments from the city of Kitchener out of about 8,000 for the whole of Canada, a fairly creditable record I think. Among those seven there were of course, no women, but one man was wrongfully interned, he being a British subject naturalized in New Zealand. Although this man was a British subject, with ample proof of naturalization from the Secretary of State of New Zealand, he was sent to the internment camp and kept there for three or four years. He was never accorded a trial, and finally, in spite of his protests, was deported to Germany but was later brought back by the Canadian Government who recognized and realized their error. I know that in the county of Waterloo, in the county of Perth, in Oxford possibly, in Bruce and Huron and Renfrew and in many sections of the Canadian West, there are thousands, almost hundreds of thousands, of the people of whom I speak now. To-day under this legislation they have no country. Surely the first privilege of a British subject is the franchise itself; and yet under this Bill the Government to-day makes outcasts of men who are innocent. They punish men who have committed no offence, because, although offences have been charged no definite statements have been given by hon. gentleman opposite who spoke before me. No proofs have been given of the broad statements which they have made with regard to the acts of treason committed by these people. If the Bill passes in its present form, this Government points the finger of scorn at a hundred thousand good Canadians and cries "Unclean." Why? Because these men and women by an accident of birth came from Germany or Austria and because they were trustful enough to accept the invitation and the promise of agents of the Government of Canada -that if they came to this" country and discharged their duty as citizens should, they would be granted all the rights and privileges of British citizenship.
Mr. Speaker, I intended to read some extracts from some of the papers in connection with this phase of the question but I will dispense with that. But, I do want to say that the whole spirit of the clause which I condemn is wrong. We have heard a good deal of the spirit of t.he bon entente that should exist between the people of Quebec and -the people of Ontario I think it is right that such a spirit should prevail, but why cannot the same spirit be extended to the small minority that lives in other provinces of Canada? And, Sir, I want to place on record my convic-

.tion that in the treatment of most of these people of former alien enemy birth, Germans .and Austrians, a sad mistake was made by many Canadiaets and by the Dominion Government. I was going to say that some of it might he excused-no not excused, but explained by reason of the prejudice and the sufferings arising out of the w.ar. But, Sir, if there had been something more of trust and a little less of suspicion it would have been very, very much better for this country. I want to say-and I know whereof I speak-that among the people of North Waterloo of German or Austrian origin-although we have not many Austrians there-there is no love of militarism and that most of them came from Europe to escape from that very thing. I want to say further that I do not believe that the common people in any part of .the world desire war, because war means the .slaughter of their sons. I do not believe that is true of any people, and it is certainly not true of the people of North Waterloo. They hate war. They want to he good Canadians,-if you will only allow them to be so.
Mr. Speaker, the Government of this country brought these people here, and they came in good faith, believing what was told them, that Canada was a democracy that welcomed all who would share her responsibilities. They toiled and helped to build up this country, including the county of Waterloo from which I come, as did also the Mennonites of whom we have heard so much. They identified themselves with us, their children attended our schools, and they absorbed our national ideals. In very truth they became of us, and we recognized the fact by entering into the sacred compact of citizenship with them. They have carried out their part of the bargain. Can an honourable nation do any less than that? If these people disobey the law they are as liable to punishment as the native born, their responsibilities are in no way lightened, and their property and industry must contribute to the national treasury.
Some eight or ten days ago I enjoyed a speech delivered in this House by the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Poster), when he made a plea for greater tolerance as between hon. members on the two sides of the House. I appreciated very much what he said. Before I resume my seat I would like to say to him, if I may, Mr. Speaker, and if a younger man may with propriety say this to an older man: That kindness and trust and charity are infinitely more pow-

erful than the degrading influences of suspicion-influences, which .are exemplified in the Bill before us to-day And I would say to him that the harvest which he can expect from the sowing anew of the seed of racial hatred will not redound to the advantage of Canada if carried out in this Bill. Canada is populated by people of diverse races. It will always be so, and you can only weld them into one great Canadian nationality by the process of education and by inculcating and applying the principles of justice and equality, and the square deal.
I do not dare to hope, Sir, that anything I may have said will induce the Government to strike out this clause, but if they do so it would he, not an act of generosity but an act of justice, for which I think they would receive full credit. But whether or not they take that course, when this Bill reaches the committee stage, if no one else moves in that direction, I certainly will move for the striking out of this disfranchising clause.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: We will be with you.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: In conclusion, Sir, I would like to say that in the ranks of the Allied nations, notably in those of the United States, there were thousands upon thousands of men of German or Austrian ancestry, and many of them held positions of high authority in that country. Yet I do not believe that the trust reposed in them was ever betrayed. But, Sir, I would like to come nearer home. From Waterloo, and from Perth, from Oxford and from Renfrew, from Bruce and Huron, and from the Great West there came hundreds of men to fight in the Canadian army, many of whom died on the battlefields of France. To-day I submit the honour of Canada is in the hands of this Parliament. I ask you not to insult the memory of these men through an affront to their sisters and brothers and to the mothers that bore them.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one clause of this Bill has been very freely discussed. I have very little to say with regard to it, but I wish to join with the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Euler) in stating that I think it is very illogical-indeed, it is still more illogical than he has shown it to be in that particular. We usually speak of what we ourselves know especially. Although there are not many people in my constituency of alien enemy birth, a number of such men homesteaded there years ago and became naturalized, they brought their children with them, many of them very young, and

I think I am correct in saying that probably more would be disfranchised among those families than those who are now entitled to vote, and yet those so disfranchised are the very people who should be entitled to vote. Those who are now entitled to vote are the people who, if any, should be disfranchised. If among those people there are any with German or Austrian sympathies they are those who had reached manhood before they settled in this country. Their children who have been educated in our Canadian schools, have acquired Canadian habits and imbibed Canadian ideals, and surely there is no disloyalty among them. If there is any disloyalty in that district it is among those who under this Act are entitled to vote. I do not know what will be said with regard to the rights of those people, but it seems to me that if a man who came from Germany or Austria is entitled to exercise the franchise, there is no good reason why his wife should not be also entitled. She is as much a British subject as he is; and his children, who were minors at the time he was naturalized, are British subjects just as much as he is. It seems to me very illogical if we disfranchise one part of the family without disfranchising the other, especially when we disfranchise those members of the family who are certainly much better Canadians than their parents who are enfranchised.
I would like to draw the attention of the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) to some other features of the Bill. By subsection (E) of section 79 the agent of a candidate must publish the list of all those who contribute anything towards the election expenses. That, I think, is a move in the right direction, and I would like to congratulate the Solicitor General on it. I am sorry, however, that he did not go a little further. It seems to me that while he was making that provision he should at the same time have provided that a list should also be published of those who contributed to the party funds at any stage of the game.
The leader of the Opposition made a remark which was apparently very well received on both sides of the House with regard to the necessity of so legislating that the people would have faith in this Parliament and in its doings. Faith is the most necessary thing in this life. You cannot succeed in any line of business without faith; you cannot carry on any commercial undertakings without faith. Indeed, without faith we can do nothing; without faith in each other we live but a life of misery. Accordingly, we must so
act that the people shall have faith in us; otherwise we cannot make the progress that we should. We must not only be entitled to the confidence of the people; we must also have that confidence. Any one who has been around the country a little knows that campaign funds are regarded with a great' deal of suspicion; in fact, there is nothing of which the people are so suspicious. I do not mean the funds that go to the agent of the candidate or to the candidate himself in order to bring about his election; I mean the campaign funds that are contributed to the party. The Solicitor General has asked for suggestions. I suggest that he go a little farther than he has gone in section 79 and compel the publication of campaign funds of every description, including funds paid to the party or contributed to any association or group of candidates. If he does that he will accomplish more in the way of inspiring public confidence in Parliament than he would be doing in carrying out the step proposed; though I do commend him for the step that he has taken; it is a step in the right direction.	.
I am sorry that the Solicitor General is not in his seat; I wanted to direct his attention to another point. In schedule A to section 32, rule (14) provides:
The onus of substantiating sufficient prima facie ground to strike off any name shall be upon the applicant.	,
The word " applicant " in that schedule is used about a dozen times, but outside of that particular section, " applicant " refers always to the man who is applying to be put on the list. The reference here would certainly seem to be to the appellant rather than to the applicant. The appellant is nowhere referred to as an applicant. The appeal is never referred to as an application; it is referred to as an appeal. If this section is allowed to stand as it is, there will be some confusion; but it would be quite a simple manner to change the word " applicant " to " appellant ".
I again emphasize the point which I have made in regard to the necessity for extending the provision set forth in section 79 for the submission of a statement respecting election expenses, so that it will require every party, every group of* politicians, every one in connection with such party or group of politicians, to make public the sources of funds contributed for all purposes in connection with party work.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the motion?

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
As I listened this afternoon to the speech delivered by the Acting Solicitor General I was expecting to hear a statement in regard to the motive and reason underlying Clause 29, and I had hoped that by this time some one would have risen on the Government side to give some information that would justify that clause as it stands. That the speech of the Acting Solicitor General was magnificent in its ensemble no one can deny, but that the whole Act was built on the principle of fairness and simplicity is a statement that I challenge both on the ground of the facts contained in the Act and the other documents to which the Act refers. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, no one in this House will attack my conduct as being inconsistent, because when I was a candidate for the Con-

servative party and was consulted as to whether disfranchisement should take place under the War-time Elections Act I protested. I believe, however, that in the result the then Government was justified in taking rigorous measures to prevent disastrous consequences; but that a condition of that sort should be perpetuated when we in Parliament are bragging about the virtues of the League of Nations and are singing of " Peace on eaith," and being made to swallow holus-bolus treaties of peace without a quorum in the House, I say that we ought to be exceedingly careful what we do if we wish to make the people of Canada believe that we are sincere and honest in our speech and in our actions. I believe that there is a good deal of misapprehension in regard to the Bill which is before us. As regards the Naturalization Act and the clause calling for ten years' residence after the termination of the war I had occasion to protest against that measure at the last session of Parliament when I said that it was shameful that we should have to enact such legislation, and the reply was that it was a universal act not applicable to Canada alone. 'I therefore accepted this explanation without further remarks. Now, however, I trust the Government will deem it its duty to have this measure changed to such an extent that men shall not be obliged to remain in Canada fourteen, thirteen, twelve and eleven years before they can be naturalized.
The statement has been made that in the past naturalization has been given too freely to some citizens of Canada through the mistakes of previous governments. This statement I do not challenge, but because mistakes have been made in the past by previous governments is no reason why this Government should go to the opposite extreme. I am going to endeavour to seek a motive in Clause 29, and I shall ascribe to that clause the best possible motive that can be conceived. If there is a reason at all in Clause 29 for disfranchising a British subject that reason lies in a naturalization act itself which requires, among other things, that the applicant for naturalization shall be of good character and shall possess an adequate knowledge of either English or French. Now, Sir, I can understand that it may be the desire of the Government to raise the standard of citizenship, and, owing to the operation of the law which made it possible for a woman to become a British subject by marriage or a son to become a British subject without naturalization, to see that such persons 
should possess the necessary qualifications, namely, good	character	and ability
in English or French. That can be the only motive behind this clause, unless there be the unworthy	motive that
we are seeking to elect ourselves once more by disfranchising as many people as possible. If that is the case, I would go a step further and say that we should disfranchise every one who voted against the Union Government and so make a sure thing of it. I believe, however, Mr. Speaker, that the real motive underlying Clause 29 is in fact to ascertain whether the man or woman affected has all the qualifications required under the Naturalization Act. But if this interpretation be correct, then it will be necessary to amend Clause 29 so as to make this motive apparent at least. Now, let us see what this clause says.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: I hope the hon. member will not go too far in discussing the details of the measure which, of course, can be discussed only in committee.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
I have not yet entered
into any details, Mr. Speaker, and I trust I may be permitted at least to broach* the general principle of the Bill, which is the question of enfranchising or disfranchising. Clause 29 does disfranchise, and I wish to call attention to this particular portion of the Act which reads, inter alia as follows:
-provided, however, that this subsection shall not apply to any person born on the continent of North America -nor to any person who in person applies to and obtains from any judge having jurisdiction in naturalization proceedings a certificate under the hand of such judge and the seal, if any, of his court, to the effect following:
The certificate is as follows:
This is to certify that from evidence submitted before me, I am satisfied that A.B.
of	in the province of	
(occupation)	is a person naturalized as a British subject by operation of law, who, but for such naturalization is qualified and would be entitled at the date of the issue of this certificate to be personally naturalized in Canada.
Now it says that if you have disfranchised a man or woman there must be a personal application for naturalization. Is Clause 29 the only procedure enacted? Can a person simply step into a court and say: I wish to be naturalized, having been disfranchised as the wife of so-and-so or the son of so-and-so? Is there any particular procedure provided as to how a person may place his or her claim before the court?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext:
The hon. member is
certainly discussing the details of the Bill

which can only properly he discussed in committee. He is not discussing the principle of the Bill, to which I shall have to ask him to confine his remarks.
Mr. H. A. MACKIiE: I hope that I am not singled out in any way because the debate has been carried on on clause 29.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: Order; if the hon. gentleman feels aggrieved at the decision of the Chair he has his remedy. The last remark which he has made is entirely uncalled for.

subsubtopic: SECOND. READING OF BILE NO. 12 MOVED BY HON. HUGH GUTHRIE.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I bow to your ruling and I will endeavour to generalize more than I have, but I desire to call to your attention once more the fact that clause 29 has been discussed on the other side and on this side as well as the clause of the Naturalization Act.
